results.answer:
As a federal retiree with an OPM annuity who isn't entitled to Social Security or RRB benefits, you must ask to have your Part B premiums deducted from your annuity. Contact your local Social Security office to make your request. Visit SSA.gov/locator to find your local office.

If you don't set up the annuity deduction, you'll get a bill for your Part B premium. Typically, Part B premiums are billed quarterly (every 3 months). There are 4 ways to pay your premium bill, including:

- Online: Visit Medicare.gov/account to log into (or create) your Medicare account, then, select "Pay my premium" to make a payment by credit card, debit card, Health Savings Account (HSA) card, or from your checking or savings account. This free service is the fastest way to pay your premium.
- Medicare Easy Pay: This free service automatically deducts your payment from an account (the excerpt cuts off here, and the other two payment methods aren't shown).

For a Self Only enrollment, your annual out-of-pocket maximum is **$7,500**: For a Self Only enrollment, your out-of-pocket maximum for eligible coinsurance and copayment amounts is $7,500 when you use Preferred providers. When your eligible out-of-pocket expenses reach this catastrophic protection maximum, you no longer have to pay the associated cost-sharing amounts for the rest of the calendar year.

A few caveats:
- Only eligible expenses for Preferred provider services count toward these limits.
- Certain types of expenses do not accumulate to the maximum. The specific list of excluded expenses isn't included in these excerpts.
- Under Basic Option, you must use Preferred providers for your care to be eligible for benefits, except in certain circumstances, such as emergency care.

To place your first order through the Mail Service Prescription Drug Program:

- Complete the initial mail order form
- Enclose your prescription and copayment
- Mail your order to CVS Caremark, P.O. Box 1590, Pittsburgh, PA 15230-1590

Alternatively, your physician may call in your initial prescription at 800-262-7890, TTY: 711.

For the first order, allow up to two weeks for delivery. For later refills, allow up to ten days for delivery.

Eligibility differs by option. Under Standard Option, members may use our Mail Service Prescription Drug Program to fill their prescriptions. Under Basic Option, the program is available only to members with primary Medicare Part B coverage.

Some drugs need extra steps. If a drug requires prior approval, the program won't fill it until approval is obtained. CVS Caremark, the program administrator, will hold your prescription for you up to 30 days. If prior approval is not obtained within 30 days, your prescription will be unable to be filled. Also, specialty drugs will not be dispensed through the Mail Service Prescription Drug Program.

results.answer:
In many cases, it's **15%** above the Medicare-approved amount. A non-participating provider can charge you more than the Medicare-approved amount, but in many cases, the charge can't be more than 15% above the Medicare-approved amount for non-participating healthcare providers. This amount is called "the limiting charge."

The Blue Cross Blue Shield FEHB brochure adds some related points:
- The Medicare Summary Notice (MSN) form that you receive from Medicare will have more information about the limiting charge. If your physician tries to collect more than allowed by law, ask the physician to reduce the charges.
- The cap doesn't apply to doctors who have opted out of Medicare. Should you visit an opt-out physician, the physician will not be limited to 115% of the Medicare-approved amount.
- If you have this plan and your physician does not accept Medicare assignment, you pay the difference between the "limiting charge" or the physician's charge (whichever is less) and our payment combined with Medicare's payment. Under Basic Option, you must see Preferred providers in order to receive benefits.

results.question: How do I appeal a decision about a claim under Original Medicare?

retrieved.documentName: Medicare & You 2027
Medicare & You 2027
Medicare & You 2027
Medicare & You 2027
Medicare & You 2027
Medicare & You 2027
Medicare & You 2027
Medicare & You 2027

results.answer:
Under Original Medicare, the appeal starts with your Medicare Summary Notice (MSN):

- Get the "Medicare Summary Notice" (MSN) that shows the item or service you're appealing.
- Circle the item(s) on the MSN you disagree with. Write an explanation of why you disagree with the decision. You can write on the MSN or on a separate piece of paper and attach it to the MSN.
- Include your name, phone number, and Medicare Number on the MSN. Keep a copy for your records.
- Send the MSN, or a copy, to the company that handles bills for Medicare (Medicare Administrative Contractor) listed on the MSN. You can include any information you have about your appeal, like information from your health care provider.

Instead of marking up the MSN, you can use Form CMS-20027. To get this form, visit Medicare.gov/basics/forms-publications-mailings/forms/appeals, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to have a copy mailed to you. TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

Deadline: You must file your appeal by the date in the MSN. If you missed the deadline for appealing, you may still file an appeal and get a decision if you can show good cause for missing the deadline, such as a disability, illness or accident that delayed you.

Decision: You'll generally get a decision from the Medicare Administrative Contractor within 60 days after they get your request. If Medicare will cover the item(s) or service(s), it will be listed on your next MSN.

Before you file, you can ask your doctor, supplier, or other health care provider for any information to make your appeal stronger. Keep a copy of everything related to your appeal, including copies you send to Medicare or your plan. You can also get help filing an appeal from your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).

results.question: Is there a cap on what I pay per month for insulin?

retrieved.documentName: Medicare & You 2027
Medicare & You 2027
Medicare & You 2027
2026 FEHB Blue Cross Blue Shield Service Benefit Plan Brochure (RI 71-005)
2026 FEHB Blue Cross Blue Shield Service Benefit Plan Brochure (RI 71-005)
Medicare & You 2027

results.answer:
Yes, under Medicare. Plans can't charge you more than $35 for a one-month supply of each Part D-covered insulin you take, and you don't have to pay a deductible for insulin. So the cap is **$35 per one-month supply of each covered insulin product**, not a single total cap across all your insulins. Similar cost limits apply for traditional insulin used in Part B-covered insulin pumps.

Separately, in 2027, your out-of-pocket costs for covered drugs are capped at $2,400. Once you (or other people or programs on your behalf, like Medicare's Extra Help) reach this limit, you'll pay $0 for your covered Part D drugs for the rest of the year.

The 2026 FEHB Blue Cross Blue Shield Service Benefit Plan brochure lists insulin, diabetic test strips, lancets, and tubeless insulin delivery systems as covered medication and supplies. However, the excerpts provided don't state a specific monthly cap for insulin under its Standard or Basic Option.

results.answer:
The yearly Part B deductible is **$283 in 2026**. Under Original Medicare, if the Part B deductible applies, you must pay all costs (up to the Medicare-approved amount) until you meet the yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026).

The documents don't clearly show which Medigap plans pay it. - Plans K and L pay 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year after you meet your out-of-pocket yearly limit and your yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026).
- You can't buy Medigap Plans C or F if you became eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020.
